No, that isn't right. A language model doesn't remember earlier conversations on its own, so your assistant won't remember last week's student unless you build that in.

**Example.** A student tells the assistant on Monday, "I finished the laser cutter training." On Friday they come back and ask, "Can I book the laser cutter?" The model sees only the text it is sent for that request. If Monday's message isn't in it, the model has no idea Monday happened. It isn't forgetting. It never had access.

**Why it feels like memory.** In a chat app, the program resends the whole conversation so far with every new message. The model reads it all again each time, so it looks like it remembers. That only works within one conversation, and only while the history fits in the context window. The context window is the maximum amount of text the model can read in one request.

**What this means for your design.** Memory is something your program does:
1. Save what matters, such as "Sam: laser cutter training done, Oct 28", in a file or database.
2. At the start of the next session, look up that student's record.
3. Put the relevant part into the prompt.

The saving and looking up are ordinary Python code. This is also why your mission asks you to decide what the assistant keeps in context and what it saves between sessions. Everything you put into the prompt also costs tokens, so you'll want to save short facts instead of whole transcripts.

**Quick check.** Suppose the assistant does save "Sam: laser cutter training done" to a database. What has to happen before the model can use that fact on Friday?

If you want, I can turn this into a lesson on context and memory, which is the next step in your mission.
